svg.text: Hips moved 7% of body height toward the ball
From address to impact. The rule table threshold is 4%.
Swing events used by the rule: address and impact
It may feel like you stay down,
but at impact your hips have moved toward the ball.

text.tspan: Early extension means your hips move toward the ball as you swing
down. At address your backside sits back over your heels. By impact
it has moved 7% of your body height toward the ball, well past the
4% the rule table allows. When the hips move in, your upper body has
to stand up to make room, so the club has less space to swing
through, and strikes can come out thin or to the right. The most
likely reason is that your lead hip does not turn far enough: it had
turned 31° at impact, where about 45° is typical. If the hips cannot
turn, they slide forward instead. The wall drill teaches your hips
to turn back and away from the ball, and the 90/90 exercise works on
the turn they need.
Something unclear?
Ask the information
desk.

svg.text: One drill and one mobility exercise

text.tspan: Set up with your backside touching a wall, or
your golf bag. Make slow half swings and keep
your trail glute on the wall through impact.
Sit with both knees bent to 90°, one leg in
front and one to the side. Rotate slowly to
switch sides, chest tall.
Generic guidance, not medical advice — see a
physiotherapist if you feel pain.
No drill: a possible fault is not a reported
fault.

I can explain your early extension
result: the measurements, the key frames,
the fault chain and the two exercises.
Ask me anything about them.
Why does it feel like I’m staying
down when I’m not?
Your chest stays bent over, so it feels
like you keep your posture. But the
impact key frame shows your hips 7% of
your body height closer to the ball than
at address. To make room, your upper body
has to stand up. The wall drill lets you
feel it: if your trail glute leaves the
wall before impact, that is the move.
